title: No Light on Eilean Mòr
summary: In December 1900 the light on the Flannan Isles went dark, and when the relief boat came on St Stephen's Day all three keepers were gone. The station was tidy, the lamp was ready and the clock had stopped, but one man's oilskins still hung on the peg. The island remembers several days at once, the 15th, the 26th and the 29th, and keeps them layered like spray on glass. The truth waits at the wrecked west landing.

lines: You'll be the lass from Breasclete. The Board men said nothing of you, and I'll say nothing either.
No flag on the staff. No boxes set out. No one on the landing.
We blew the horn till the captain's ears rang. He fired a rocket. Nothing came down that hill.
I went up alone. Somebody had to.
The gate was shut. The house door was shut. Like they'd stepped out a minute since.
I'll not lie to you, miss. I came down a deal faster than I went.
The clock on the kitchen wall had stopped.
Have you ever stood in a house where the clock's stopped and nobody's come to wind it?
The fire was dead. Ashes cold for days. The beds were empty.
And one set of oilskins on the peg. Just the one. Two gone.
Take it. The gate key.
I'll not go through that gate again till the boat's men come up with me.
Mind the bare staff in the yard.
Go to the house first. But if the door's fast, ask at the old chapel.
The island keeps what the wind drops.

A faint green light breathes inside, though there is nothing in there that could burn.
Shepherds went in on their knees to pray for a safe landing, and a safe going.

lines: You came up the hill with your head covered, lass. We never did that here.
Bare the head. Turn with the sun. Thank Him who let you land.
Murdo, they called me. Of Uig. That is near enough to a name for this place.
You do not say the true names of things on this rock. It is listening.
We called it the Country, out here. Never by its own name.
What is named, it keeps. And the Board-men wrote their names in a book every day.
On the fifteenth the gale came over the top of the island like a black wall.
The wind brought something from the Board-men's house that day and laid it in the hollow by the door.
There, at the right of the chapel doorway, where we left our bits of bread.
Take it. They will not be needing it.
When you go west, do not answer the one in the water.
He asks in rhyme, and he waits for you to stumble.

lines: No time for the coat. There's no time for the coat.
You'll be from Breasclete. I know that black you're wearing.
I was only the Occasional, standing in for Ross. I'd no business being on this rock at all.
Dinner was done. James washed, Tom dried. Same as any day.
The glass was falling. You could hear the sea working at the west side.
James and Tom got into their oilskins. Something at the west landing wanted seeing to.
They went down. I stayed by the fire.
After a while I looked out. West.
And I saw... I saw what was coming up out of the sea.
I ran. I never stopped for the coat. There was no time for the coat.
The tower door's fast. You'll be wanting the lamp, I think.
James keeps the key in his sea-chest in the bedroom, under his Bible.

props.name: great beehive lens of glittering prismatic glass rings in a polished brass frame, a dark unlit paraffin lamp at its heart

lines: The lamp at the heart of the lens.
Wick trimmed. Fountains filled. Every inch of brass polished bright.
It was made ready for the night of the 15th.
No one came up the stair to light it.
Deep in the prisms you think you see a spark of amber.
You blink, and it's only grey light on glass.

props.name: framed duty slate hanging on a hook, columns chalked in a steady hand

lines: Wind. Weather. Lamp lit. Lamp out.
Chalked up neatly, day after day, to the morning of 15 December.
After that there is nothing. No one came back to write the afternoon.

props.name: tall lantern window in black iron astragals, fog-grey Atlantic far below, white spray bursting over a distant cliff landing

lines: Far below, through the fog, the west landing.
White water explodes over it again and again, higher than the cliff edge.
The superintendent keeps his back to this pane.
The wind presses at the glass.
For a moment it sounds like a man shouting a name you can't quite catch.

props.name: small pine work table holding a black cloth-bound logbook, a brass oil can and folded polishing cloths

lines: The logbook, bound in black cloth.
Plain entries in a plain hand: weather, lamp, stores, the work of the station.
No prayers. No weeping. Whatever the stories will claim, the men wrote nothing strange here.

props.name: pinned Northern Lighthouse Board notice in copperplate on yellowed paper

lines: NORTHERN LIGHTHOUSE BOARD.
The steamer Archtor, passing on the night of 15 December, reports that the Flannan light could not be seen.
Storms held the relief at Breasclete until the 26th.
Eleven days of darkness, and no one could come.

upper turns of a black cast-iron spiral stair climbing a whitewashed shaft into darkness

lines: The iron stair winds on up the shaft into grey half-light.
Three men climbed it every evening to light the lamp. The treads are worn bright in the middle.

props.name: pine wall rack of spare glass lamp chimneys with brass paraffin cans on its lower shelf

lines: Spare chimneys, every one polished clear.
The cans filled to the brim. The Board's order, kept to the last.

props.name: wooden crate of paraffin tins stencilled N.L.B.

lines: Paraffin tins, enough to see a winter through.
Enough for every night of the eleven the light stood dark.

props.name: wooden crate of paraffin tins stencilled N.L.B.
small brass paraffin hand lamp, its glass chimney glowing low

lines: A small hand lamp, burning low.
It wasn't lit when you came through the door. You're almost sure of it.

props.name: oily polishing rags dropped on slate

art.description: grey-whiskered man in a dark Northern Lighthouse Board uniform coat with brass buttons and a peaked cap, spectacles, notebook and pencil in his hands, faintly translucent like a memory
idle: standing writing in his notebook, looking up over his spectacles

lines: Everything is in order. That is what troubles me most, miss.
Everything is in order.
I came out on the twenty-ninth to see for myself.
I knew these men. I chose them myself.
The slate is written up to the morning of the fifteenth. Then nothing.
The lamp was cleaned, filled and trimmed, ready for the night.
They meant to light it. Whatever took them, it took them before dusk.
Two sets of oilskins are gone. The Occasional's still hangs in the kitchen.
The west landing is wrecked.
The box of ropes kept in a crevice a hundred and ten feet above the sea is gone. Its ropes are strewn over the rocks.
Iron railings bent. A stone of a ton moved from its place.
Turf torn away higher up the cliff than I'd have believed.
My opinion is this. They went down that afternoon to secure the rope box.
MacArthur saw something from the house and ran after them, coat or no coat.
And an enormous sea came up and took all three.
No one can know it for certain. But I believe it.
Here. The key to the west gate.
I've seen it once. I'll not see it again.
Go and look for yourself, if you must, and keep well back from the edge.

A torn clod lies at the foot, roots still wet.
By most accounts the scars run some two hundred feet above the sea.
No wave should reach so high.
The sea came over the top of this island.

lines: The iron railings are wrenched landward, the uprights bent over like grass after a flood.
Muirhead found them so: bent, displaced, torn from their sockets.
Iron this thick does not bend in the wind.
Only water of terrible weight could do this. And it came from below.

It belongs in the rope box at the west landing, a hundred and ten feet down.
The sea tore it from the box and flung it up here.

characters.name: The Blue Man of the Sea

art.description: tall gaunt sea spirit with blue-grey skin, long beard of white foam and weed, arms too long, pale sea-glass eyes, water pouring off him, his lower body dissolving into a column of churning surf
idle: swaying in the surf, long arms hanging, head tilted mockingly
moving: wading forward through the surf, long arms reaching out

lines: Woman in black on the shelf of stone, what do you seek where the gale has blown?
Three came down and I kept all three...
Two wore the oilskins and one ran bare... say me the rest, if you dare, if you dare.
Ropes for the Board and a box for the sea... come to the edge, and I'll answer thee.

parts.art: black-leaded cast-iron landing crane with a riveted jib swung idle, hook and chain hanging, sound and greased

lines: The west landing crane, bolted fast to its granite plinth.
Sound. Greased. Not so much as a scratch on it.
Harvie guessed they drowned trying to secure a crane.
But the crane is untouched. The men did not die for the crane. They died for a box of rope.

props.name: the empty rope-box crevice

parts.art: deep black crevice split into a gneiss cliff, its rock hollow empty where a wooden rope box once stood, frayed wet ropes trailing out of it

lines: A cleft in the cliff, about a hundred and ten feet above the sea.
The rope box was wedged in here, safe from any ordinary sea.
The hollow is empty. Its ropes and tackle trail out across the rock like hair.
This is what they came down to save.

lines: Board-issue rope, torn from the box and flung across the shelf.
It lies where the sea dropped it, still dripping.

props.name: the displaced stone block
props.material: dressed grey granite trim, steps and copings

lines: A dressed block of stone, a ton or more, gouged out of its bed and set down here askew.
Muirhead could not believe it when he saw it.
Nothing on this island could have moved it.
Nothing but water.

props.name: section of iron railing folded flat and twisted by the sea

lines: Iron railings, folded down flat to the rock as if something enormous had stepped on them.
Muirhead found them bent like this. Only water of terrible weight could do it.

black oilskin sou'wester hat lying dropped on wet rock

lines: A black oilskin sou'wester, dropped on the wet rock.
It belonged to one of the two who went down dressed for the weather.
The third man had no coat and no hat. He had no time.

props.name: the frozen wave

parts.art: towering grey-green wall of Atlantic seawater frozen mid-rise, streaked with white foam, taller than a cliff

lines: The sea stands up out of the west in a grey-green wall, higher than the cliff.
It does not fall. The island has held it like this, in the light of that afternoon.
An enormous, unexpected sea, higher than any keeper would think possible.
It is the most likely answer. No one will ever know for certain.

ambient.art: single falling drop of grey-green seawater

art.description: semi-transparent ghost of a steady bearded keeper in his forties in black oilskins and sou'wester, hands braced as if on a rope box, rimmed in cold sea-green light, water streaming from his hem
idle: standing braced, turned to face the viewer

lines: You came down the west path. Good lass. Mind the edge.
The Board's ropes, lass. You don't let the sea have the Board's ropes.
We came down after dinner to make the box fast. The weather was getting up. Nothing we'd not seen before.
The lamp's trimmed. Fountains full, wick cut square, brass polished.
I meant to be back up to light it at dusk.
Tell them at Breasclete it was quick. Tell them the lamp was ready.
My name, lass. Say it when Donald asks.
The rock has kept it long enough.

art.description: semi-transparent ghost of a younger clean-shaven lighthouse keeper in black oilskins, sou'wester blown back, coils of rope over his shoulder, rimmed in cold sea-green light, water dripping from him
idle: standing holding the rope coils, glancing anxiously at the viewer

lines: Five shillings, they docked me, last time the sea took gear.
I wasn't having it twice.
So down we came, James and I, in our oilskins, with the wind in our teeth.
We never even heard it coming. You'd think you'd hear a thing that size.
A hundred and ten feet up, that box. No sea comes that high.
That's what we told ourselves.
Donald will ask you for our names. Say mine plain.
I'd like to hear it once more in a living mouth.

art.description: semi-transparent ghost of a broad dark-haired keeper with no coat, in a soaked collarless shirt and open waistcoat, frozen mid-stride running, one arm flung out ahead, mouth open in a shout, rimmed in cold sea-green light
idle: frozen mid-run, arm flung out toward the cliff, shouting

lines: I saw it from the house. I shouted. I ran.
I never got the coat.
Look at it, lass. Look how high it stands. I was halfway down before I knew I'd left the door open.
Say our names, lass. This rock takes everything that has no name.
It took the box. It took the day. It took us, and it keeps us nameless, like everything else on it.
Say them aloud, all three, and it has to give us back.

dialogue.speaker: You
lines: James Ducat.
Thomas Marshall.
Donald MacArthur.

dialogue.speaker: The island
lines: The wind takes the names off your lips and carries them out over the water.
Behind you, on the high top, something warm kindles.
An amber beam swings out across the Atlantic, over the rock, over the standing sea.
When it passes, the three men are gone, and the rock is only rock.

dialogue.speaker: The island
lines: The record will say that no one can know for certain.
The island has shown you its most likely truth. No monster, and no murder.
Only three men who went down to save the Board's ropes, and a sea that came higher than any sea should.
